title: Rehras close
hook: morning Japji, evening Rehras: the day is held at both ends

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rehras with others, and your line, end the day together. Did you share a minute with someone at day's end? Today we close Rehras, on our sixteenth day with it. Day four hundred twenty.
screen: `REHRAS WITH OTHERS — END THE DAY TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Look at a shelf of books. Take away one bookend, and the row starts to lean. Take away both, and the books slide over in a heap. Put a bookend back on each side, and the whole row stands up straight, every book in its place, even the thin ones in the middle. Nothing in the middle has changed. It's just held at both ends. That's the shape of the Sikh daily prayers. Today: Rehras close.
screen: `A SHELF OF BOOKS.` → `NO BOOKENDS: THE ROW SLIDES.` → `HELD AT BOTH ENDS, IT STANDS.`

segments.voice: Sikhs call the daily prayers nitnem, the daily rule. In the morning, the Japji of Guru Nanak and the other morning banis. In the evening, Rehras. And at night, as we'll see tomorrow, Kirtan Sohila. Two bookends and a nightlight. Look back at what we packed for the road. Rehras opened at the door: so dar, what is that door, where everything sings. Hearsay calls You great; only one who has seen can say. Saying it I live, forgetting I die. Then So Purakh, that Being without stain. You are the true Creator, the river everything flows in. The pool of fire and water, feet stuck in the mud, and a hand from those who remember. This human body is your chance. A humble plea, with the word rahraas hidden inside. Why worry, mind, when even the rock-creatures eat? Then the Tenth Guru's Chaupai: shelter for the night. The Anand's joy, and a plate of truth, contentment and contemplation. Ardas, standing, asking that all be well. Dusk itself, sandhiaa, as a practice. And the prayer said together. So what is Rehras for? The morning Japji sends a person out into the day. Rehras gathers them back in, with the same Name and many of the same Gurus. The hours in the middle, the thin books on the shelf, the commute, the meetings, the dishes, stand up straight because they're held from both sides. Both ends held.
screen: `NITNEM: THE DAILY RULE.` · `THE DOOR, HEARSAY, REMEMBERING, SO PURAKH.` · `THE MUD, YOUR CHANCE, THE PLEA, WHY WORRY.` · `CHAUPAI, ANAND, ARDAS, DUSK, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `BOTH ENDS HELD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set a bookend at each end of today. Think of this morning. Was there a beginning, any beginning: a line, a breath, a moment before the phone? If there was, remember it. If not, that's fine. Now think of tonight. Choose your bookend: a line of Rehras, the first line of the Chaupai, the Anand's joy has come, or just a minute of quiet before sleep. Decide it now, and decide tomorrow morning's too. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, for both. The bell holds the time.
Rehras close. Sixteen days with the Sikh evening prayer: nine shabads, the Chaupai, the Anand, the Mundavani and Ardas, holding the day's far end as the Japji holds its start.
Your line: both ends held. Today, keep one bookend at each end of the day, however small. Tomorrow, the night song. Day four hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Sikh nitnem frames the day: the Japji and other banis in the morning, Rehras Sahib in the evening when work is done, and Kirtan Sohila at night before sleep.

match.prompt: Rehras, looking back — tap the pairs.

myth: the Sikh day has prayers only in the morning
the Japji in the morning, Rehras in the evening, Kirtan Sohila at night.
Rehras ends with the Mundavani and a slok, often followed by Ardas
after the nine shabads, the Chaupai and the Anand.
Rehras is made only of hymns by Guru Nanak
it has shabads by Guru Nanak, Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, the Anand of Guru Amar Das, and the Tenth Guru's Chaupai.

fork.setup: a friend asks why Sikhs pray in the evening if they already prayed in the morning. what would you say?
options: the morning prayer wears off by noon.
the morning sends you out; the evening gathers you back: the day is held at both ends.
it's a penalty for a bad day.
fork.reveal: Japji at dawn and Rehras at dusk are bookends: the hours in the middle stand up straight because they're held from both sides.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nitnem, the daily rule; the set prayers that frame the Sikh day, morning, evening and night.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rehras is just the evening version of morning prayers.
what it means: its own prayer, packed for the road, that gathers the day back in as the Japji sent it out.

what a scholar hears: Rehras gathers five Gurus' voices, Guru Nanak, Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, Guru Arjan and Guru Gobind Singh, and ends with passages that come at the close of the Guru Granth Sahib.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, on nitnem: morning banis, Rehras and Kirtan Sohila
Rehras shabads, Ang 8–12; Anand, Ang 917–922; Mundavani and slok, Ang 1429

notes: Block E close (days 405–420): the teach names each day's line. Also the week-end look-back for days 414–420.
Voices in Rehras: Guru Nanak, Guru Ram Das, Guru Arjan (shabads, Mundavani, slok), Guru Amar Das (Anand), Guru Gobind Singh (Chaupai, savaiya, dohra): five Gurus. Confirm.

Audit (2026-10-01): the review said 'sixteen days after we opened it', but day 405 to day 420 is fifteen days; it now says 'our sixteenth day with it'. The practice no longer tells everyone to pray; it invites a bookend, with prayer optional.
